subject: Help please - unmarked distsamp models returning NAs for SE, Z and P(>|z|) values, not sure why?

messages.author: 77fa2bc3ece64945
messages.subject: Help please - unmarked distsamp models returning NAs for SE, Z and P(>|z|) values, not sure why?
parts:
Hello,

Me again!  I had a problem before with the fatalists not working - see https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/2gFDCwKsiSM/

I now have my final model, but looking at it I realised that it is returning NAs for the SE, Z and P(>|z|) values and I have no idea why.  I hoped you all might be able to help me figure it out.  I have put in the code below and the model outputs and can share the data or answer any questions if needed.

I chose a haxard rate detection function as it had a lower AIC than the half-normal and is deemed more reliable than the negative exponential.  When I noticed the NAs I reran it with a half normal and it comes out with measures for the SE, Z and P(>|z|) values.  I also tried a negative exponential function and this also had NAs.  Additionally, when I try display an output with means parameterization it returns NAs.  To try and understand why I ran models where I removed each covariate on the density side and it did not return NAs models where I removed LCCode which is a factorial land cover classification and MKL10mBuff which is a continuous measure of elevation.  

All continuous variables have been standardised using the scale function. 

Any insights very much appreciated.

Cheers,

Gwili


### For posting to unmarked Google Group

library(unmarked)
mk <- read.csv("mk_dungsveg_standardised_200319.csv", header = TRUE)
mk$MK_slope_r <- as.factor(mk$MK_slope_r)

### Package things up into an unmarkedFrame ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

              "DistAllRoa", "DistRdNoTr", "DistCultiv", "DistPlanta", "DistSettle", "DistRiver", "DistBound", "bio14_wc30", "bio12_wc30", 
              "bio16_wc30", "bio17_wc30", "mi_wc30s", "pr_1_wc30s", "pr_2_wc30s", "pr_3_wc30s", "pr_4_wc30s", "pr_5_wc30s", "pr_11_wc30",

              "pr_wet2_gg", "mimq_wc30s", "miaq_wc30s")]
mk$area <- (mk$Effort_m_T*9)     
mk.umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=as.matrix(mk[,11:15]),
                          siteCovs=data.frame(covs),
                          dist.breaks=c(0, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5),
                          tlength = mk[,10],
                          survey="line",
                          unitsIn="m")

### Final model 22/3/19----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I now have my final model, but looking at it I realised that it is returning NAs for the SE, Z and P(>|z|) values and I have no idea why.  I hoped you all might be able to help me figure it out.  I have put in the code below and the model outputs and can share the data or answer any questions if needed.

I chose a haxard rate detection function as it had a lower AIC than the half-normal and is deemed more reliable than the negative exponential.  When I noticed the NAs I reran it with a half normal and it comes out with measures for the SE, Z and P(>|z|) values.  I also tried a negative exponential function and this also had NAs.  Additionally, when I try display an output with means parameterization it returns NAs.  To try and understand why I ran models where I removed each covariate on the density side and it did not return NAs models where I removed LCCode which is a factorial land cover classification and MKL10mBuff which is a continuous measure of elevation.  

All continuous variables have been standardised using the scale function. 

Any insights very much appreciated.

Cheers,

Gwili

Dear Gwili,
 This is a tough problem and I imagine to sort it out would require that someone roll up their sleeves and take a good hard look at your data, which would be time consuming and hence no one is volunteering to do it.
 There is always a general issue of difficult likelihood estimation when you have a very large model, which you do. In these cases you can expect very unstable solutions and sensitivity to starting values, depending on whats in the model and what is not. I suspect this is your problem.  
 If you have done so already , I suggest building up your model one-covariate at a time and also I recommend against using the hazard model during the build-up phase since the extra parameter is more difficult to estimate.  Finally, you might get rid of some of the habitat covariates. With so many covariates I would recommend doing a PCA on the set of them and reduce to just a few.

regards
andy

parts: So, when I run my final model with all the covariates, as below, I have no problems:

I think there may actually be some problems with this model, as several of the landcover levels have huge standard errors. I would be hesitant to use those results.

The small number of sites for some landcovers could definitely be an issue. My approach would be to subset your data to retain only sites in the most common landcover classes (say, # of sites >30), confirm that I get a reasonable-looking model fit, and then iteratively add the remaining landcovers back until the large standard errors and/or NAs reappear. That should at least narrow down if landcover is the problem and if so which levels are causing it.

I'd also experiment with using an effects parameterization (by removing the `-1` from your formula) to see if you get better convergence with that.

Ken

So, when I run my final model with all the covariates, as below, I have no problems:

 

I think there may actually be some problems with this model, as several of the landcover levels have huge standard errors. I would be hesitant to use those results.

 

The small number of sites for some landcovers could definitely be an issue. My approach would be to subset your data to retain only sites in the most common landcover classes (say, # of sites >30), confirm that I get a reasonable-looking model fit, and then iteratively add the remaining landcovers back until the large standard errors and/or NAs reappear. That should at least narrow down if landcover is the problem and if so which levels are causing it.

 

I'd also experiment with using an effects parameterization (by removing the `-1` from your formula) to see if you get better convergence with that.

 

Ken

So, when I run my final model with all the covariates, as below, I have no problems:

 

I think there may actually be some problems with this model, as several of the landcover levels have huge standard errors. I would be hesitant to use those results.

 

The small number of sites for some landcovers could definitely be an issue. My approach would be to subset your data to retain only sites in the most common landcover classes (say, # of sites >30), confirm that I get a reasonable-looking model fit, and then iteratively add the remaining landcovers back until the large standard errors and/or NAs reappear. That should at least narrow down if landcover is the problem and if so which levels are causing it.

 

I'd also experiment with using an effects parameterization (by removing the `-1` from your formula) to see if you get better convergence with that.

 

Ken
